recipe.history:
The carrot is one of the most widely cultivated root vegetables in the world, but its origins are far removed from the bright orange roots we recognize today. Wild carrots — Daucus carota — originated in Central Asia, specifically in the region of present-day Afghanistan, where purple, yellow, and white varieties grew in rocky hillside soils thousands of years ago. The orange carrot, now so iconic that it has become synonymous with the vegetable itself, was actually a relatively late development — Dutch horticulturalists in the seventeenth century selectively bred orange-pigmented varieties, possibly as an homage to the House of Orange-Nassau, though the historical evidence for this nationalist theory is more romantic than rigorous. What is certain is that the Dutch carrot trade transformed the vegetable's genetics and spread orange varieties across Europe and eventually the world. Ancient Greeks and Romans knew the wild carrot primarily as a medicinal plant — its seeds were used as a digestive aid and, controversially, as a contraceptive — and it was only gradually that cultivation shifted toward the fleshy, sweet taproot we eat today. Carrot tops — the feathery, aromatic greens — were as prized in ancient kitchens as the root itself, used in ways similar to parsley and dill, and their return to contemporary cooking represents a recovery of knowledge that was never truly lost, only temporarily forgotten.

Carrots arrived in the Americas with European colonists in the early seventeenth century and quickly adapted to New World soils, becoming a staple of both kitchen gardens and farm cultivation. In American cuisine, the carrot long occupied a humble supporting role — a component of mirepoix, a side dish for pot roast, a stock ingredient — rarely given the opportunity to lead. This began to change in the 1970s and 1980s with the rise of vegetarian and health-conscious cooking movements, which elevated the carrot to a starring ingredient in dishes from carrot cake to carrot soup. The farm-to-table revolution of the 1990s and 2000s further transformed the carrot's culinary status: chefs began working with heirloom varieties — Chantenay, Danvers, Cosmic Purple, Dragon — and discovering that different cultivars had dramatically different flavor profiles, from the floral sweetness of yellow carrots to the peppery earthiness of purple. Carrot-top pesto, inspired by Italian cucina povera's tradition of using every part of the plant, entered upscale American restaurant menus as an expression of whole-vegetable cooking philosophy. Carrot-ginger preparations, drawing on the long relationship between ginger and carrot in Southeast Asian and South Asian cuisines, became a staple of aiolis and dressings, their complementary sweetness and spice creating a combination that felt simultaneously exotic and deeply familiar on an American burger.

I have a specific memory tied to carrots that I have never been able to fully shake. I was at a Sunday farmers market, the kind with mismatched canopy tents and dogs on leashes and somebody's kid selling lemonade that tastes mostly like sugar water. A farmer had a table loaded with bunches of rainbow carrots, still dirty from the field, their tops wild and green and voluminous as bouquets. I bought three bunches because they were cheap and beautiful, and when I got home I had no idea what to do with the tops — I had always thrown them away. I pinched off a feathery frond and chewed it and found it tasted like parsley crossed with carrot, slightly bitter, faintly sweet, with a clean herbal finish. I got out the food processor and made a pesto with the tops — walnuts, garlic, lemon, Parmesan, good olive oil — and tasted it and laughed out loud in my empty kitchen because it was so good. The carrot ribbons I made by drawing a vegetable peeler lengthwise down the raw carrots over and over until I had a pile of translucent, curling strips that I tossed with rice wine vinegar and sesame oil. The aioli came together with carrot juice and grated fresh ginger and a whisked egg yolk. I ate the whole burger in about four minutes and stood there wondering how many years I had been throwing away the best part of the carrot.

There is a philosophical dimension to cooking a burger to medium rare that goes beyond mere preference or technique — it is about respect for the animal and the farmer and the craft. When you grind fresh beef and form it into a patty, you are working with a living tissue that has spent months accumulating flavor, fat, and moisture. The intramuscular fat — the marbling — begins to render at around 130 degrees Fahrenheit, softening and lubricating the surrounding muscle fibers, creating that characteristic juicy, almost creamy texture that makes a great burger taste fundamentally different from a meatloaf. When you cook beyond 140 degrees, into medium-well territory, those fat deposits have fully liquefied and drained away, the muscle fibers have tightened and squeezed out their moisture, and you are left with a patty that is structurally sound but sensorially diminished. The carrot preparations on this burger — the bright, herbaceous pesto, the crisp acidic ribbons, the warm-spiced aioli — are calibrated against the richness of a properly cooked medium rare patty. A well-done patty would flatten the whole composition into something dull and one-dimensional. Medium rare keeps it alive.
ingredients: 3 1/2 cups (440g) bread flour, plus more for dusting
6 tbsp (85g) unsalted butter, softened and cubed
2 cups (50g) fresh carrot tops (feathery fronds only, thick stems discarded), washed and dried
4 large carrots (mixed colors if available), peeled
1/4 cup (60ml) fresh carrot juice (store-bought or juiced from 2–3 carrots)
1 tbsp fresh ginger, finely grated (about a 1-inch piece)
1 small clove garlic, minced to a paste with salt
1 1/2 lbs (680g) freshly ground beef (80% chuck / 20% brisket blend)
2 tbsp unsalted butter, softened (for toasting buns)
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BRIOCHE BUNS — DAY BEFORE or at least 5 hours ahead: Combine flour, sugar, and salt in the bowl of a stand mixer with the dough hook. Bloom yeast in warm milk for 5 minutes until foamy.
2. Add milk-yeast mixture and eggs to flour. Mix on low 2 minutes until shaggy. Increase to medium and knead 5 minutes until smooth.
3. Add softened butter one cube at a time on medium-low speed, fully incorporating each piece before adding the next, about 8–10 minutes total. Dough will be soft, glossy, and slightly tacky.

4. Transfer to a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and refrigerate overnight or let rise at room temperature 2 hours until doubled. Divide into 4 portions (roughly 170g each), shape into smooth balls, place on a parchment-lined sheet, cover, and proof 1 1/2–2 hours at room temperature.
5. Brush with egg wash. Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 16–18 minutes until deep golden brown. Cool completely on a rack.

6. MAKE THE CARROT-TOP PESTO: Bring a small pot of water to a boil. Blanch carrot tops and parsley for 30 seconds to reduce bitterness and preserve bright color. Transfer immediately to an ice bath. Drain and squeeze out excess moisture thoroughly.

7. Combine blanched greens, toasted walnuts, garlic, Parmesan, lemon zest, and lemon juice in a food processor. Pulse until coarsely ground. With the motor running, drizzle in olive oil until the pesto reaches a spreadable, slightly chunky consistency. Season with salt and pepper. Transfer to a jar and press plastic wrap directly onto the surface. Refrigerate until needed.

8. MAKE THE CARROT RIBBON SALAD: Using a Y-peeler or vegetable peeler, draw the peeler down the length of each carrot with firm, steady pressure to create long, wide ribbons. Continue until each carrot is fully ribboned. Transfer to a bowl.

9. Whisk together rice wine vinegar, sesame oil, honey, and salt. Pour over carrot ribbons and toss gently. Let marinate at room temperature 20–30 minutes. Just before serving, toss with sesame seeds and cilantro leaves.
10. MAKE THE CARROT-GINGER AIOLI: Combine egg yolks and Dijon mustard in a medium bowl and whisk vigorously 1 minute. Combine neutral oil and olive oil in a liquid measuring cup.

11. Begin adding oil drop by drop, whisking constantly, until the emulsion forms and thickens (first 3–4 tablespoons are critical). Once emulsified, add remaining oil in a slow, thin stream, whisking continuously.

12. Add carrot juice, grated ginger, garlic paste, apple cider vinegar, lemon juice, and salt. Whisk until fully incorporated. Taste and adjust seasoning. Refrigerate in an airtight container until needed. Aioli will keep up to 3 days.

13. FORM THE PATTIES: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 170g each). Gently press each into a patty about 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick. Press a shallow dimple in the center. Season both sides with kosher salt, black pepper, and smoked paprika. Rest 15 minutes at room temperature.
14. COOK THE PATTIES: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add neutral oil. Lay patties in the pan and sear undisturbed 3 minutes until a deeply browned crust forms. Flip once.

15. Place one slice of sharp white cheddar on each patty. Tent with foil. Cook 2–3 minutes more until internal temperature reaches 130–135°F (54–57°C) on an instant-read thermometer. Remove from heat and rest 3 minutes on a rack.
16. TOAST THE BUNS: Slice brioche buns. Spread cut sides with softened butter. Toast cut-side down in the same pan over medium heat 60–90 seconds until golden.

17. ASSEMBLE: Spread a generous layer of carrot-top pesto on the bottom bun. Place the cheddar-topped patty on the pesto. Spoon a liberal amount of carrot-ginger aioli over the melted cheddar. Pile a tangle of marinated carrot ribbons on top. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt and crown with the top bun. Serve immediately.
